summary: Deep dive on recurring OOMs and intermittent CUDA timeouts seen during long-context workloads. Discussed KV cache behavior, batching configs, quantization tradeoffs, and retry semantics across hosted/dedicated/private deployments. Agreed on a set of logs and bench runs to validate mitigations and a canary schedule.
topics: batching strategy and sequence length distributions
transcript:
[00:00] Sofia: all right everyone thanks for joining, yes this is Sofia from Redwood, joined by Devon and Marcus. How's everyone doing?
[00:07] Laura: good thanks, we have some folks on video but yeah excited to dig in weve been seeing intermittent OOMs in prod jobs.
[00:12] Devon: yeah thanks Laura, can you remind us of the failing workload? long context retrieval plus summarization, avg seq 6k tokens but tails up to 20k.
[00:20] Ethan: correct, most requests 4-8k but we do have the occasional up to 20k for docket processing. We are on Dedicated GPUs (A100-80GB) but still hit OOMs after a few hours under load.
[00:31] Rama: and sometimes we see CUDA timeouts rather than a neat OOM log, like C-U-D-A driver reset messages, then clients retry and get 500s.
[00:40] Sofia: ok, good context. we'll try to map sequence to memory pressure, kv-cache behaviour, and batching. quick clarifying q: are you using prefix caching between requests?
[00:48] Ethan: yes we enable K-V cache at the route level, but we suspect the cache growth is unbounded for some sessions. maybe stale keys.
[00:55] Devon: that matches what we've seen — if cache entries dont evict (TTL or per-session GC) the KV store can grow and use host/GPU memory depending on implementation.
[01:05] Laura: I should mention quantization was turned on for smaller perf delta, we use 4-bit quant for majority of models to save memory. not sure if that affects kernel behavior.
[01:15] Marcus: quantization reduces model param memory but can introduce different kernel paths that use more scratch/interop memory during attention which can still cause spikes.
[01:23] [01:30] Devon: ok i'll sketch a hypothesis: long-tail sequences + large batch coalescing + idempotent KV growth -> sustained GPU mem fragmentation -> occasional allocation failure -> kernel triggers device-side timeout -> driver reset. Some retries are aggressive and amplify load.
[01:42] Laura: is there any known issue with CUDA alloc patterns and long-lived KV caches?
[01:46] Devon: yes, when KV cache is stored as contiguous tensors per session, if sessions accumulate and we do frequent memcpy to device we can fragment device memory. also certain older CUDA drivers have slower cudaMalloc behavior under high fragmentation.
[01:58] Rama: we see the resets mostly during peak batch windows around 09:00 and 16:00. interestingly the first crash in the hour is often an OOM, subsequent ones are driver timeouts.
[02:10] Sofia: makes sense. let's talk retry semantics — do you have client-side retries? what backoff?
[02:16] Ethan: our infra has a simple 3x immediate retry policy in the SDK, so when a single request fails we blast it again which could worsen the spike.
[02:24] Devon: immediate retries are a common anti-pattern here. Recommendation: exponential backoff with jitter, and for non-idempotent requests ensure dedupe keys or at-least-once semantics are handled upstream.
[02:35] [02:45] Laura: can we change SDK behaviour easily? we've got a deployed client in customer devices that expects quick retry.
[02:50] Sofia: yes, but we can also implement server-side per-route circuit breakers: short-term reject/queue when memory headroom drops below threshold. Marcus?
[02:58] Marcus: yep, we can expose a per-route headroom config and a soft-fail policy: return 429 with Retry-After, or reroute to smaller quantized model automatically.
[03:10] Ethan: reroute is interesting, does Redwood support automatic fallback to a quantized variant?
[03:15] Devon: yes we have model variants. automatic fallback is possible: route policies can choose lower-memory variant under pressure. caveat: differences in output quality.
[03:24] Laura: quality is a concern, but we'll accept lower quality for degraded cases. more worrying is root cause; what logs should we send?
[03:31] Devon: start with device logs (dmesg / kernel GPU errors), nvidia-smi -q snapshots over time, CUDA driver logs, and Redwood side: per-request memory footprint, KV cache size per session, batch composition traces, and timeline of kernel durations.
[03:44] Rama: we have dmesg and driver logs from one incident, and can capture nvidia-smi sampling. i'll upload them.
[03:50] [04:00] Sofia: great. let's also discuss warmup and KV eviction strategies — are you pre-warming KV for expected sessions?
[04:06] Ethan: not currently. we just let cache populate organically.
[04:09] Devon: that can create thundering-herd patterns — when many sessions request long-tail tokens they all populate KV causing memory spike. Warmup + TTL or LRU eviction is recommended.
[04:20] Laura: is there auto-eviction in Redwood? we thought TTLs were per-route but not sure.
[04:25] Marcus: we support per-session TTLs and global cache size limits. defaults are permissive. we can advise conservative defaults for your workload.
[04:33] [04:40] Ethan: what about batching — you mentioned coalescing. are there knobs to limit batch size or max tokens per batch?
[04:46] Devon: yes, runtime exposes max_batch_size and max_total_tokens_in_batch. For long-tail distributions, cap on total tokens prevents a single huge request from blowing up the per-batch memory.
[04:57] Laura: but capping batch or tokens increases latency — that's a tradeoff.
[05:01] Sofia: exactly, it's latency vs safety. we should pick SLOs where tail latency increases but OOMs stop.
[05:08] [05:15] Devon: another mitigator: per-request streaming so we can start consuming output while freeing KV pages if possible. also async eviction of cold sessions.
[05:24] Rama: is fragmentation vs high water mark more likely? i mean does fragmentation cause allocation failure despite free total memory?
[05:30] Devon: yes fragmentation can cause failure; diagnostic: if total free memory is large but cudaMalloc of a big contiguous tensor fails, that's fragmentation. cudatoolkit and our allocator metrics can show max free block size.
[05:43] Laura: good to know. can we change the allocator? jemalloc for host — but for device?
[05:49] Marcus: we use a custom device allocator built on top of cudaMallocAsync on recent runtimes; older stacks fall back to cudaMalloc. cudaMallocAsync with a persistent pool tends to reduce fragmentation.
[05:59] [06:05] Ethan: huh we are on driver 470.x, maybe time to upgrade. any known driver-specific regressions?
[06:12] Devon: some older drivers had slower reclaim and worse fragmentation under heavy small-allocation churn. upgrading to newer stable drivers (>=520) and using cudaMallocAsync can help. we'll share recommended driver matrix.
[06:24] Laura: can we run a repro? we have a staging cluster mirroring prod. what script should we run?
[06:30] Devon: we'll provide a stress script that simulates seq-length distribution and KV population patterns, includes large spike scenarios, and records nvidia-smi sampling, allocator histograms, and kernel latencies.
[06:43] [07:00] Sofia: quick note on timeouts: some of the timeouts youre seeing are OS-level watchdogs because kernels run longer than the OS timeout — TDR on Windows or watchdog on Linux. those show as driver resets.
[07:14] Rama: our resets log says watchdog. yes.
[07:17] Devon: we try to keep per-kernel durations bounded by splitting long attention computations where possible. for some models it's doable with chunked attention, for others we revert to smaller model variants.
[07:29] Laura: chunked attention — does Redwood runtime support that automatically?
[07:33] Marcus: for several model families we have kernel alternatives: standard attention or memory-efficient attention. runtime chooses based on sequence length and hardware. but switching at runtime has cost; needs eval.
[07:45] [07:50] Ethan: what about quantization interaction — we saw more timeouts after enabling 4-bit, odd.
[07:56] Devon: quantized kernels sometimes use int8/bitpacked ops that change memory access patterns; they can be faster but may use extra scratch buffers for dequant/pack which increases transient memory pressure. we'll quantify that in the bench.
[08:09] Laura: ok. any immediate mitigation we can apply with low risk?
[08:14] Devon: immediate: change client retries to exponential backoff with jitter; lower max_batch_size and cap max_tokens_in_batch; enable per-route KV TTL of e.g., 30m with LRU eviction; temporarily disable aggressive quantized variant for longest-context routes; upgrade CUDA driver and enable cudaMallocAsync if OS/drivers permit.
[08:33] [08:40] Rama: we'll prioritize retries change and TTL.
[08:43] Sofia: good. i'll list out the logs we need. Devon will share the stress script and driver compatibility sheet.
[08:50] [09:00] Laura: can we also get per-request memory metrics produced by Redwood in the logs? we dont currently have that in app telemetry.
[09:07] Marcus: yes we can enable per-request memory sampling for a short window in staging — it adds low overhead. we'll turn it on for the canary.
[09:16] Ethan: you mentioned reroute to smaller model — how transparent is that wrt API? do we need client changes?
[09:22] Devon: no client changes if done server-side; route maps model variants and returns same schema. we'll include an indicator header in responses when fallback occurred.
[09:31] [09:40] Laura: about retries — how to handle non-idempotent calls (generation with side-effects)?
[09:45] Devon: for non-idempotent flows use idempotency keys and dedupe on server. if that's not possible, use stricter backoff and consider 429 soft-failure to avoid duplicate processing.
[09:57] Sofia: OK sounds like consensus on action items. quick logistics: we'll collect logs and run stress runs this week and schedule a follow up next week.
[10:06] Rama: timeline works.
[10:08] Devon: last technical note: watch for fragmentation via allocator metrics — if max contiguous block size drops below ~model-weight-chunk we should preemptively fail or reroute.
[10:19] Laura: makes sense. thanks.
[10:22] [10:30] Sofia: any other questions?
[10:31] Ethan: one more — we have a VPC Private deployment in future. does the behavior differ on Private vs Dedicated?
[10:38] Marcus: Private on-prem can have different driver/kernel combos, and network artifacts matter less for pure GPU OOMs; but if private uses different cgroups or host allocators you can see different fragmentation, so tests are required per environment.
[10:51] Laura: ok we'll run in both staging Dedicated and our early Private cluster.
[10:55] Sofia: perfect. i'll email the checklist and share the stress script. thanks everyone.
[10:59] [11:00] Meeting ends — recording stopped.
